lessons.title: Never run out of content ideas: a systematic ideation process with Claude
lessons.summary: Build a repeatable prompt that turns your niche, past top performers, and real audience questions into a running list of specific, on-brand content ideas.
lessons.goal: Generate 20+ specific, on-brand content ideas from your niche and real audience signals in one session, using a prompt you can rerun every week.
lessons.whyItMatters: Staring at a blank content calendar is the single most common reason creators go quiet. Generic 'give me content ideas' prompts return generic ideas — the same ten everyone in your niche already sees from ChatGPT. Building a repeatable ideation prompt that's grounded in your actual niche, your past top performers, and the real questions your audience asks turns idea generation from a creative struggle into a five-minute weekly habit.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a Claude account, plus a short list of: your niche/topic, 3-5 pieces of content that performed well for you (or comparable creators), and any recurring questions or comments from your audience.
steps: Open a new chat in Claude.
Write down your niche in one sentence, plus who you're making content for.
Gather 3-5 of your best-performing past posts or videos (or note you don't have data yet).
List any recurring questions, comments, or DMs you get from your audience.
Use the ideation prompt below with these inputs.
Ask Claude to group the ideas by content pillar or funnel stage.
Star the 5 ideas you could realistically film or write this week and save the rest for later.
Save this prompt so you can rerun it weekly with fresh inputs.
lessons.prompt:
You are helping me build a content idea list. Do not give me generic ideas anyone in this niche could post — every idea must connect to a specific detail I give you below.

My niche: [YOUR NICHE, e.g. "budgeting and money management for freelancers"]
My audience: [WHO, e.g. "new freelancers 1-3 years in, anxious about irregular income"]
My best-performing past content (topic + why it worked, if known): [PASTE 3-5 EXAMPLES OR WRITE "no data yet"]
Recurring questions/comments from my audience: [PASTE REAL QUESTIONS, COMMENTS, OR DMs]
Formats I create in: [e.g., short-form video, long-form YouTube, newsletter, carousel posts]

Generate 20 content ideas. For each one:
1. A specific title or hook (not a vague topic label)
2. Which content pillar it belongs to
3. Which input above it's grounded in (a past hit, a specific audience question, or a clear niche gap) — do not include an idea that isn't traceable to one of my inputs
4. Best format for it from my list

Group the 20 ideas under three headers: "Answers a question my audience already asked," "Builds on a topic that already worked," and "Fills a gap I haven't covered yet." Flag any idea that would work better as a personal story than a how-to.
lessons.explanation: Requiring every idea to trace back to a specific input — a real question, a proven topic, or a named gap — is what keeps this from producing the same generic list any creator in your niche would get. Grouping by 'why this idea earns its place' instead of by topic gives you a built-in prioritization: ideas answering questions people already asked tend to convert best, so start there. Flagging story-shaped ideas separately matters because a how-to prompt and a personal-narrative prompt need different scripting approaches, which the next lesson covers.
lessons.example:
Niche: budgeting for freelancers. Audience question logged from comments: "how do you save for taxes when your income changes every month?" Past hit: a video on tracking irregular income that got unusually high saves.

Expected output includes an idea like "The 3-account system I use to never get surprised by a tax bill (even with unpredictable income)" under "Answers a question my audience already asked," explicitly citing the comment as its source — not a generic "5 budgeting tips for freelancers" idea with no traceable origin.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, gather your real niche, audience questions, and 3-5 past posts (or note you're starting fresh), then run this prompt and star the 5 ideas you'll actually make this week.
lessons.expectedResult: A list of 20 specific ideas, grouped by why each one should work, with at least 5 you can commit to producing in the next seven days.
commonMistakes: Skipping real audience questions and only giving Claude a topic, which produces the same generic ideas as everyone else's list.
Treating all 20 ideas as equally worth making instead of prioritizing the ones grounded in real signals.
Not saving or rerunning the prompt — ideation is a weekly habit, not a one-time list.
Ignoring the 'no data yet' option and inventing fake past performance instead of being honest about what you actually know.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running note on your phone where you paste any audience question or comment the moment you see it — by the time you run this prompt each week, you'll have a fresh, real list instead of trying to remember comments from memory.

lessons.title: Turn a content idea into a script or outline that sounds like you, with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Draft a script or outline from your idea and a sample of your own writing, so the result sounds like you instead of a generic AI voice you have to rewrite.
lessons.goal: Produce a script or outline for one piece of content, in your own voice, that needs light editing rather than a full rewrite.
lessons.whyItMatters: The biggest complaint creators have about AI-written scripts is that they all sound the same — overly enthusiastic, full of stock phrases like 'let's dive in,' and nothing like how the creator actually talks. Feeding ChatGPT a real sample of your own voice and locking the structure to your idea (not letting it invent a different angle) is what separates a script you can read verbatim from one you have to rewrite from scratch.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have one content idea ready (from your ideation list), plus a short sample of your own writing or a transcript of yourself talking on camera — 100-200 words is enough.
steps: Open ChatGPT and start a new chat.
Paste a short sample of your own voice — a transcript, caption, or past script you wrote yourself.
State your content idea and the format (script for video, outline for a post/newsletter).
Use the drafting prompt below with both inputs.
Read the draft out loud (for video scripts) to catch anything that doesn't sound like you.
Ask for one targeted revision at a time rather than a full regeneration.
Save the approved script or outline alongside your idea list.
lessons.prompt:
Here is a sample of my own writing/speaking voice:
[PASTE 100-200 WORDS OF YOUR OWN WRITING OR A TRANSCRIPT OF YOU TALKING]

Match this voice exactly — including sentence length, how formal or casual I am, and words I'd actually use. Do not add hype phrases like "let's dive in," "game-changer," or "in today's video" unless they appear in my sample.

Content idea: [YOUR IDEA/HOOK]
Format: [short-form video script / long-form video script / written post outline / newsletter outline]
Key points I want covered: [LIST 2-5 POINTS]
Length target: [e.g., 60 seconds spoken / 800 words / 5 outline sections]

Write the [script/outline]. For a script, include a hook in the first 3 seconds and write it as spoken sentences, not written prose. For an outline, use headers with a one-line note under each on what goes there. Do not introduce a new angle or claim I didn't ask for.
lessons.explanation: Pasting a real voice sample gives ChatGPT a concrete target instead of an abstract adjective like 'casual' — the same principle that makes tone-matching work in general writing, applied specifically to scripts. Explicitly banning generic hype phrases removes the most common tell of AI-written content. Requiring 'spoken sentences, not written prose' for video scripts matters because text that reads well on a page often sounds stiff out loud — asking for it directly avoids a rewrite pass just to make it speakable.
lessons.example:
Voice sample: a casual, slightly dry caption where the creator uses short sentences and self-deprecating humor. Idea: "the 3-account system I use to never get surprised by a tax bill." Format: 60-second short-form script.

Expected output: a script opening with a punchy, specific hook in the creator's own rhythm (not "Hey guys, welcome back!"), covering the 3 accounts as spoken lines, ending on a direct call to action — all readable aloud in roughly 60 seconds without sounding like a script written by someone else.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, pick one idea from your ideation list, paste a real sample of your own voice, and generate a script or outline with this prompt.
lessons.expectedResult: A script or outline in a voice recognizably yours, needing only light editing, that hits your target length when read aloud or scanned.
commonMistakes: Skipping the voice sample and asking for 'a casual tone,' which still produces generic AI phrasing.
Letting the script drift into a different angle than your original idea.
Not reading video scripts aloud before filming, missing sentences that look fine on paper but are awkward to say.
Requesting a full regeneration for a small fix instead of a targeted one-line edit.
lessons.proTip: Build a small file of 3-4 voice samples from different moods (energetic, calm, instructional) and paste the one that matches the specific piece you're writing — one single 'voice sample' won't cover every type of content you make.

lessons.title: Repurpose one piece of content into ten platform-native posts with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn a single long-form piece — a video, article, or newsletter — into ten posts that each feel native to their platform instead of a copy-pasted excerpt.
lessons.goal: Turn one long-form piece of content into ten platform-specific posts across short-form video, carousel, and text formats without losing the core idea or repeating yourself verbatim.
lessons.whyItMatters: The highest-leverage habit in content creation is making one piece of content work ten times, but a caption pasted unchanged from YouTube into Instagram, or a script excerpt dropped straight into a LinkedIn post, reads as lazy and underperforms. Repurposing well means re-forming the same core idea for how each platform is actually consumed — a guardrailed prompt keeps the facts identical across all ten while genuinely adapting format and tone.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have your source piece ready — a transcript, script, or full text of the long-form content you're repurposing.
steps: Paste your full source content (transcript, article text, or detailed summary) into Claude.
Identify the single core idea or takeaway you want preserved across every repurposed piece.
Use the repurposing prompt below, specifying your platforms.
Review each output for platform-native formatting (hook style, length, hashtag conventions) rather than a resized copy of the source.
Check that no post adds a claim or detail that wasn't in the source.
Adjust hooks in your own voice before scheduling.
Batch-schedule the ten posts across the days following the original piece's release.
lessons.prompt:
Here is my source content, a [video transcript / article / newsletter]:
[PASTE FULL SOURCE TEXT]

Core idea I want preserved across everything: [ONE SENTENCE]

Repurpose this into 10 platform-native posts. Do not just shorten or copy-paste sections — genuinely reformat each one for how people actually consume that platform, while keeping every fact and claim traceable to the source above (do not add new information).

Produce:
1. 3 short-form video scripts (under 45 seconds spoken, each with a different hook/angle on the core idea, [VISUAL: ...] cues)
2. 2 carousel/slide post outlines (5-7 slides each, one point per slide)
3. 2 single-image or text-post captions (under 150 words, platform-casual tone)
4. 2 LinkedIn-style posts (more context/insight framing, under 200 words, minimal hashtags)
5. 1 short newsletter blurb (under 100 words) promoting the full piece with a link placeholder

For each, note which specific part of the source it's drawn from. Vary the hooks across all 10 — no two should open the same way.
lessons.explanation: Explicitly banning 'shortening or copy-pasting' and requiring genuine reformatting is the core instruction — without it, models default to trimming the source rather than rebuilding it for each platform's actual consumption pattern. Requiring a source citation per post lets you audit that nothing was invented while spreading one piece across ten formats. Demanding varied hooks across all ten prevents the common failure of every repurposed post opening with the same line, which flattens your reach across platforms since the same follower sees the same hook everywhere.
lessons.example:
Source: a 12-minute video transcript on 'the 3-account system for irregular income,' covering why one account fails, how the 3 accounts work, and a real numbers example. Core idea: "separating income, taxes, and spending into 3 accounts removes the guesswork."

Expected output: three differently-hooked short scripts (one opening on the numbers example, one on the common mistake, one as a direct how-to), two carousels breaking down the 3 accounts step by step, two captions in different casual openers, two LinkedIn posts framing it around freelance financial planning, and a newsletter blurb teasing the full breakdown — each citing which part of the transcript it pulled from, no invented statistics added.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, take one piece of long-form content you've already published (or a script you've written) and repurpose it into all 10 formats with this prompt.
lessons.expectedResult: Ten platform-native drafts from a single source, each traceable to the transcript, with genuinely different hooks rather than ten copies of the same sentence.
commonMistakes: Publishing all ten with identical opening lines, which trains your audience to skip your content on sight.
Letting a repurposed post add a stat or claim that wasn't in the original piece.
Treating carousel and caption formats as interchangeable instead of respecting slide-based versus scroll-based reading.
Posting all ten the same day instead of spacing them to extend the piece's reach over the following week.
lessons.proTip: Keep a swipe file of your three best-performing hooks per platform and paste them as style references in this prompt — it teaches Claude your actual hook patterns instead of generic ones.

lessons.title: Design thumbnails and visuals that get clicks with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Generate scroll-stopping thumbnail and visual concepts with ChatGPT's GPT Image 2, using a structured brief that keeps composition clean and on-brand instead of generic AI-art output.
lessons.goal: Generate 3-5 usable thumbnail or visual concepts for one piece of content using ChatGPT's GPT Image 2, with a brief specific enough to avoid generic, off-brand results.
lessons.whyItMatters: Thumbnails and cover images are often the single biggest lever on click-through rate, but image generators default to generic, oversaturated 'AI art' aesthetics unless you constrain them — busy compositions and a look that doesn't match your channel. GPT Image 2 is a reasoning-based model that plans composition and lays out text before rendering, which makes it a stronger instruction-follower than older tools, but it still needs a structured brief covering composition, color, text legibility, and brand consistency to become a real part of your thumbnail workflow instead of a novelty.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a ChatGPT account open in a chat (Plus or higher gives you the most reliable access to GPT Image 2 generation). Know your channel's usual color palette and thumbnail style, if you have one, plus the title or topic of the piece you're designing for.
steps: Write down the exact title or hook text you want featured (if any) — GPT Image 2 renders text more reliably than older image tools, but still check every generated word against your exact wording before trusting it.
Note your channel's usual style: color palette, whether faces/emotion are typically featured, level of visual complexity.
Use the thumbnail brief prompt below in ChatGPT, describing composition and mood rather than a vague topic.
Generate 3-5 variations and compare them against a real feed or grid, not in isolation, to judge scroll-stopping power.
If any element looks off — a color, a prop, rendered text — ask ChatGPT to fix just that part in the same chat; its iterative in-chat editing keeps the rest of the composition intact.
Pick the concept with the clearest single focal point, not the busiest one.
Save the winning style as a reusable prompt template for future thumbnails in the same series.
lessons.prompt:
Generate a thumbnail/cover image concept for a piece of content using GPT Image 2.

Topic/title: [YOUR TITLE OR HOOK]
Platform and dimensions: [e.g., YouTube 16:9, Instagram 1:1, Pinterest 2:3]
Mood/emotion to convey: [e.g., curious, urgent, calm, surprised]
Brand style: [YOUR COLORS, e.g., "warm oranges and cream, minimal, one clear subject"]
Composition: one clear focal point in the [left/right/center] third, leaving negative space for a text overlay in the opposite third. Avoid busy backgrounds, extra objects, or clutter that competes with the subject.
Style reference: [e.g., "photographic, not illustrated" or "flat vector illustration" — be specific, don't leave it generic]

Avoid: stock-photo-looking generic people, oversaturated colors that don't match my palette, more than one focal subject. Leave the negative space empty — do not render my title text into the image, I'll add it separately for exact font and brand control.

Generate 3 variations at different compositions (subject left, subject right, subject centered with symmetric negative space) so I can compare which reads best at small thumbnail size.
lessons.explanation: Naming a mood and a specific compositional layout — subject in one third, negative space in the other — is what produces an image that actually works as a thumbnail rather than a nice-looking picture with nowhere to put your title text. GPT Image 2 plans composition and text placement before rendering, which is why it follows a layout instruction like this far more reliably than older diffusion-only models — but instructing it to leave the negative space empty rather than attempting your exact title keeps you in control of font, size, and brand consistency, which still matters more than whatever it would render on its own. Generating three compositional variations, not three random restyles, lets you compare like-for-like and pick based on what reads clearly at small size — which is the actual test a thumbnail has to pass.
lessons.example:
Title: "The $3,200 mistake I made my first year freelancing." Mood: relieved/confident. Brand style: warm oranges and cream, minimal. Composition: subject left third, negative space right.

Expected output: three image variations showing a single clear subject (e.g., a stylized invoice or a simple wallet icon) positioned left, right, and center respectively, in warm orange and cream tones, with genuinely empty space in the opposite third for the title text to be added afterward — not a cluttered scene mixing charts, coins, calculators, and a stock photo face all at once.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, generate 3 thumbnail composition variations for a real upcoming piece of content using this brief, then check how each looks shrunk down to actual feed/thumbnail size.
lessons.expectedResult: Three to five thumbnail concepts with a single clear focal point and genuine negative space for text, at least one of which is usable with minimal further editing.
commonMistakes: Judging thumbnails at full generated size instead of shrunk down to how they'll actually appear in a feed or search results.
Letting GPT Image 2 render your title text directly without checking it matches your brand font — safer to add legible, on-brand text in a proper design tool afterward.
Accepting a busy, multi-subject composition because it looks impressive rather than because it reads clearly at a glance.
Skipping the brand-style constraint, producing a thumbnail that looks great alone but breaks visual consistency with your channel.
lessons.proTip: Once you land on a composition and palette that performs well, save the exact prompt wording as a template and only swap the topic/mood fields — consistent thumbnail style across a channel builds recognizability faster than a fresh design every time.

lessons.title: Storyboard short-form video concepts with Gemini
lessons.summary: Turn a content idea into a shot-by-shot short-form video concept using Gemini's Veo 3.1, with a brief specific enough to produce a usable rough cut — with synced audio — instead of generic stock-style clips.
lessons.goal: Produce a shot-by-shot concept and a first Veo 3.1-generated rough cut for one short-form video idea, ready for you to review, trim, and add your own voiceover or captions.
lessons.whyItMatters: Gemini's Veo 3.1 can produce usable B-roll, concept visuals, and full short clips with native synchronized audio, but a vague prompt like 'a video about budgeting' returns generic stock-footage-style output with no relationship to your actual script. Treating Veo 3.1 as a storyboarding and B-roll partner — with a shot list tied to your script's actual beats — gets you footage you can genuinely use instead of clips you generate once and discard.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have your short-form script or outline ready (from an earlier scripting session), and access to Veo 3.1 through the Gemini app on a Google AI Pro or Ultra plan (or Google's Flow filmmaking tool) — there's no meaningful free tier for video generation.
steps: Break your script into its individual beats or lines — each beat becomes one potential shot.
For each beat, decide whether you need a real Veo-generated clip, a simple text/graphic overlay, or footage you'll film yourself.
Use the shot-list prompt below in Gemini to turn your script into a structured shot list with Veo 3.1 generation prompts for each beat.
Generate one clip at a time in Veo 3.1 rather than the whole video at once, so you can review and adjust each before moving on.
Check every generated clip against your script's factual content — reject any clip that visually implies something not true (e.g., a specific dollar amount, a real place, a specific product).

Assemble approved clips with your own voiceover, captions, and any real footage in your editing tool — Veo generates its own ambient audio, so decide per clip whether you're keeping that or muting it under your voiceover.
Note which prompts produced usable results so you can reuse that phrasing for future videos in the same style.
lessons.prompt:
Turn this script into a shot list for a short-form video, with a Veo 3.1 generation prompt for each shot that needs one.

Script:
[PASTE YOUR FULL SCRIPT]

Visual style: [e.g., "clean, minimal, soft natural light" or "bold, high-contrast, fast cuts"]
Duration target: [e.g., "45 seconds total, 6-8 shots"]

For each line or beat of the script, output:
1. The script line it corresponds to
2. Shot type (Veo-generated B-roll / text-graphic overlay / footage I'll film myself) — recommend Veo generation only for generic visual concepts (e.g., "hands writing in a notebook"), never for anything requiring a specific real fact, number, product, or place
3. If Veo-generated: a specific generation prompt describing subject, action, camera angle, lighting, and any ambient sound to include, since Veo 3.1 generates synchronized audio along with the visual — no vague prompts like "a person budgeting"
4. Approximate shot length in seconds

Flag any beat where a Veo-generated clip would risk implying a specific fact (a dollar figure, a named brand, a real location) that should instead be shown as a text graphic or filmed for real.
lessons.explanation: Mapping the shot list directly to the script's own beats keeps every generated clip purposeful instead of decorative filler disconnected from what's actually being said. The explicit rule to reserve Veo generation for generic visual concepts — and flag anything implying a specific fact — matters because Veo 3.1's realism and native synchronized audio are exactly what make a confident-looking but entirely fabricated 'receipt,' 'app screen,' or 'location' dangerous to leave in a final cut. Asking for an ambient-sound note in every generation prompt is worth doing specifically because Veo 3.1 generates audio alongside video by default — deciding upfront whether you want its ambient sound or plan to mute it and lay your own voiceover avoids a messy final mix.
lessons.example:
Script beat: "Most people keep one account and hope for the best." Visual style: clean, minimal, soft light.

Expected output: shot type "Veo-generated B-roll," generation prompt like "a single empty glass jar sitting alone on a plain wooden table, soft window light from the left, static camera, shallow depth of field, quiet room tone only, no dialogue, 3 seconds" — generic and safe to generate. A later beat like "I moved $340 into taxes last month" would be flagged to use a text-graphic overlay instead of Veo, since a generated clip could visually imply an inaccurate real number or screen.
lessons.exercise: In the Gemini app, take one script from your content plan, generate the shot list with this prompt, and produce at least 2-3 approved Veo 3.1 clips for beats it flagged as safe.
lessons.expectedResult: A complete shot list mapped to your script with generation-ready prompts, and at least a few genuinely usable Veo 3.1 clips — with audio decisions already made — ready to assemble with your own voiceover and captions.
commonMistakes: Using Veo-generated video for beats that imply specific facts, numbers, or real products, which can visually mislead viewers.
Writing vague generation prompts ('a video about saving money') and accepting whatever generic result comes back.
Generating the whole video in one pass instead of reviewing and approving shot by shot.
Forgetting that Veo's generated audio still needs your own voiceover, captions, and pacing layered on top to feel like your content rather than a stock reel.
lessons.proTip: Build a personal library of your best-performing generation prompts by visual style (e.g., 'clean minimal object shots,' 'abstract motion backgrounds') — and if you need a very specific starting frame, generate it first with Gemini's native image generation, then feed that image to Veo 3.1 as the first frame to animate for tighter control over the opening shot.

lessons.title: Build your content operating system: calendar, batching, and consistency with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn your ideation, scripting, and repurposing habits into one repeatable weekly system — a calendar, a batching schedule, and a checklist — so consistency doesn't depend on motivation.
lessons.goal: Design a personal content operating system — a weekly calendar, a batching schedule, and a standing checklist — that turns the workflows from earlier lessons into a repeatable system instead of one-off tasks.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most creators don't fail from lack of ideas or writing skill — they fail from inconsistency, because every piece of content is treated as a fresh, from-scratch project. A documented operating system that says exactly what happens on which day, how many pieces get batched together, and what 'done' means for each stage is what separates creators who post reliably for years from those who burn out after a strong month. This lesson turns the ideation, scripting, repurposing, and visual workflows from earlier lessons into one system you actually run every week.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a sense of your current output (how many pieces you post per week per platform), your available working hours, and which of the earlier workflows (ideation, scripting, repurposing, visuals) you've already been using.
steps: List your current platforms and realistic posting frequency for each — not an aspirational number.
List the actual time you have available for content work per week, broken into rough blocks (e.g., 2 hours Monday, 3 hours Thursday).
Use the system-design prompt below with these constraints.
Review the proposed weekly schedule against your real calendar and flag any block that's unrealistic.
Ask for a one-page checklist version you can print or pin, covering each stage from idea to published post.
Run the system for two full weeks before changing anything — consistency beats optimization early on.
After two weeks, ask ChatGPT to help you diagnose which stage is actually the bottleneck using your real notes on what worked and what didn't.
Adjust only the bottleneck stage, not the whole system, and keep running it.
lessons.prompt:
Help me design a realistic content operating system, not an aspirational one.

My platforms and current/target posting frequency: [e.g., "YouTube: 1x/week, Instagram: 5x/week, Newsletter: 1x/week"]
My real available working hours for content per week: [e.g., "6 hours total: 2 hrs Monday morning, 3 hrs Thursday afternoon, 1 hr Sunday"]
Workflows I already use: [e.g., "weekly ideation prompt, scripting, repurposing one long piece into shorts"]
Biggest current bottleneck: [e.g., "I have ideas but rarely finish scripts" or "I make content but forget to post consistently"]

Design:
1. A weekly schedule mapping each of my available time blocks to one specific stage (ideation, scripting, filming/generating visuals, editing, batching, scheduling) — do not assume hours I didn't list.
2. A batching plan: how many pieces of content to produce per batching session for realistic output given my hours, not an idealized number.
3. A one-page checklist per content piece, from idea to published, that I can reuse every time.
4. One specific recommendation directly addressing my stated bottleneck.

Be honest if my stated posting frequency isn't achievable in my stated hours — tell me what frequency actually fits, don't just force my target into the schedule.
lessons.explanation: Anchoring the system to real hours and current bottlenecks — rather than an aspirational posting frequency — is what makes it something you can actually run instead of another plan you abandon in week two. Explicitly instructing ChatGPT to say when your target isn't achievable is the key guardrail: a people-pleasing planning tool will happily map five weekly YouTube videos onto three available hours, which sets you up to fail and then blame yourself instead of the plan. The reusable one-page checklist turns 'make content' into a series of small, checkable stages, which is what actually gets a full batch finished instead of stalling halfway.
lessons.example:
Platforms: YouTube 1x/week, Instagram 5x/week. Hours: 6/week. Bottleneck: has ideas, rarely finishes scripts.

Expected output: an honest note that 1 YouTube video plus 5 native Instagram pieces per week in only 6 hours is tight, with a schedule like Monday (2 hrs): ideation + scripting for the week's YouTube video; Thursday (3 hrs): filming/generating visuals + batching all 5 Instagram pieces from the repurposed video; Sunday (1 hr): scheduling everything for the week. The bottleneck recommendation might suggest scripting immediately after ideation in the same block, before momentum drops, rather than treating them as separate sessions on different days.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, use your real platforms, hours, and current bottleneck to generate a weekly system and checklist, then run it unchanged for two full weeks.
lessons.expectedResult: A written weekly schedule and one-page checklist matched to your actual available hours, plus one concrete change targeted at your real bottleneck — not a generic 'post daily' plan.
commonMistakes: Designing a system around an aspirational posting frequency instead of your real available hours.
Changing the system every few days instead of running it unchanged for at least two weeks to see what actually breaks.
Trying to fix every stage at once instead of targeting the one real bottleneck.
Skipping the checklist and relying on memory for what 'done' looks like at each stage, which is where consistency quietly slips.
lessons.proTip: After two weeks, don't ask 'how do I do more' — ask ChatGPT to help you identify which single stage ate the most time relative to its output, and fix only that one. Systems break at one weak link at a time, not everywhere at once.

lessons.title: Turn one strategy document into a month of posts with Claude
lessons.summary: Feed your content strategy document into Claude and generate a full month of platform-tagged post ideas and drafts, grounded in your actual pillars and goals instead of generic suggestions.
lessons.goal: Turn an existing content strategy document into a full month of post concepts, each tagged to a pillar, platform, and goal, in one working session.
lessons.whyItMatters: Social media managers usually already have a strategy document — content pillars, brand voice guide, campaign goals — but translating it into 20-30 individual scheduled posts by hand every month is where the real time goes. A prompt that treats your strategy doc as the source of truth, rather than asking the AI to invent a strategy, produces a month of posts that's actually on-brief instead of generically 'engaging.'
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have your content strategy document ready — content pillars, target audience, brand voice notes, and this month's specific goals or campaigns, if any.
steps: Gather or export your strategy document (pillars, audience, voice guide, goals for the month).
Note which platforms you're posting to and how often for each.
Use the monthly-plan prompt below with your strategy doc pasted in full.
Review the plan for even distribution across your pillars — flag if one pillar is overrepresented.
Ask Claude to flag any post idea that doesn't clearly map to a stated pillar or goal.
Export the plan into your scheduling tool or content calendar.
Note which week needs real drafted captions first versus which can stay at concept-level for now.
lessons.prompt:
Here is my content strategy document:
[PASTE FULL STRATEGY DOC: pillars, audience, brand voice notes, this month's goals/campaigns]

Platforms and posting frequency: [e.g., "Instagram 5x/week, LinkedIn 3x/week, TikTok 4x/week"]

Build a month of post concepts (roughly 4 weeks) using only the pillars, goals, and voice described above — do not introduce a new content pillar or campaign angle that isn't in the document. For each post, give me:
1. Week and platform
2. Content pillar it maps to (must match one from my document)
3. A specific concept/hook (not a vague topic label)
4. Format (static, carousel, short video, article/text post)
5. Which stated goal it supports (awareness, engagement, conversion, etc. — as named in my document)

Group the output by week. Flag any week where one pillar is overrepresented and the others are thin, and suggest a rebalance. If my document doesn't specify enough detail for a given platform, say so explicitly rather than inventing strategy to fill the gap.
lessons.explanation: Locking the output to pillars and goals that already exist in the strategy document — and explicitly forbidding new ones — is what keeps this from drifting into generic social media advice disconnected from the actual brief a client or team approved. Asking for a pillar-balance check across the month catches the common failure where one easy pillar (like 'behind the scenes') quietly dominates the calendar while a harder one (like 'product education') gets skipped. Requiring the tool to say when the strategy doc lacks enough detail, rather than quietly inventing direction, keeps the gap visible so you can go get real input instead of publishing something no one actually approved.
lessons.example:
Strategy doc pillars: 'product education,' 'customer stories,' 'behind the scenes,' 'industry commentary.' Platforms: Instagram 5x/week, LinkedIn 3x/week.

Expected output: a week-by-week table where, for example, Week 1 Instagram includes a carousel under 'product education' explaining one feature, a LinkedIn post under 'industry commentary' reacting to a named trend from the doc, and a flag if 'customer stories' has zero posts scheduled across the whole month while 'behind the scenes' has six.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, paste your real (or a practice) strategy document and platform list, and generate a full month of post concepts with this prompt.
lessons.expectedResult: A four-week plan of specific, pillar-tagged post concepts distributed across your platforms, with any pillar imbalance or strategy gaps called out explicitly rather than silently filled in.
commonMistakes: Pasting only a partial strategy doc, which produces a plan that looks complete but is missing key context.
Letting one easy-to-write pillar dominate the month without checking the balance.
Accepting an invented campaign angle that isn't actually part of the approved strategy.
Generating the whole month at concept-level and never returning to draft real captions before the first posts go live.
lessons.proTip: Keep your strategy document as a live file you update monthly, and rerun this prompt fresh each cycle — a stale strategy doc pasted into a new month's prompt is the fastest way to end up with off-brief content.

lessons.title: Write platform-native captions and hooks with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn one post concept into captions and hooks that actually fit how each platform is read, instead of one caption pasted everywhere with the character count trimmed.
lessons.goal: Write a caption and hook for one post concept, correctly adapted to a specific platform's actual reading pattern and conventions.
lessons.whyItMatters: A caption that performs on Instagram often underperforms on LinkedIn or X, not because the idea is wrong but because each platform has a different attention pattern, hook convention, and caption length that actually gets read. Managers under deadline pressure default to writing one caption and trimming it for other platforms — this lesson builds the habit of asking for genuinely platform-native versions instead.
steps: Start with one post concept and its core message.
Pick the specific platform you're writing for first.
Use the caption prompt below, naming the platform explicitly rather than asking for 'a caption.'
Ask for 3 hook variations before picking one, rather than accepting the first line generated.

Check the caption length and format against what that platform's algorithm and audience actually reward (e.g., a longer LinkedIn post with a strong first line versus a short punchy Instagram caption).
Repeat for each additional platform, changing only the platform field — don't reuse the same caption across platforms.
lessons.prompt:
Write a caption for a social media post.

Platform: [Instagram / LinkedIn / TikTok / X / Facebook — name exactly one]
Post concept/core message: [YOUR CONCEPT]
Brand voice: [e.g., "direct, a little playful, no corporate jargon"]
Goal: [awareness / engagement / drive traffic / conversion]
Call to action: [WHAT YOU WANT THE READER TO DO]

Write it specifically for how people actually read on this platform — respect its typical caption length, hook convention (first line has to earn the rest of the read), and formatting norms (line breaks, hashtag placement and count, emoji use). Give me 3 different hook/opening line options, then the full caption using the strongest one. Do not write a generic caption that could be pasted onto any platform unchanged.
lessons.explanation: Naming exactly one platform, rather than asking for a caption in general, is the single biggest lever here — it forces the model to apply that platform's actual conventions (LinkedIn's front-loaded first line before the 'see more' cutoff, TikTok's conversational caption style, Instagram's line-break rhythm) instead of defaulting to a lowest-common-denominator caption. Requiring three hook options before committing to one mirrors how a real caption gets chosen — the first line is the highest-leverage sentence in the whole post, worth testing before the rest is written around it.
lessons.example:
Concept: announcing a new feature that lets users export reports as PDF. Platform: LinkedIn. Goal: awareness. CTA: comment with what report type they want next.

Expected output: three hook options built for LinkedIn's feed-preview cutoff (e.g., a specific pain-point opener, a numbers-led opener, a question opener), then a full caption using the strongest one, written with LinkedIn's longer-form, insight-framed tone rather than a short punchy Instagram-style line — with the comment-prompting CTA placed at the end.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, take one real post concept and generate platform-native captions for two different platforms separately, comparing how differently they turn out.
lessons.expectedResult: Two genuinely different captions for the same concept, each matching its platform's real reading pattern, with three tested hook options behind the one you chose.
commonMistakes: Writing one caption and only trimming length for other platforms instead of asking for a platform-native rewrite.
Accepting the first hook option without comparing it to the alternatives.
Ignoring platform-specific hashtag and formatting norms (e.g., heavy hashtag use on a platform where it reads as spam).
Forgetting to state the brand voice, producing a caption that's platform-appropriate but doesn't sound like the account.
lessons.proTip: Keep a short 'voice cheat sheet' of words and phrases the brand does and doesn't use, and paste it into the brand voice field every time — it keeps captions consistent even across different platforms and different days of work.

lessons.title: Draft engagement replies in brand voice with Claude
lessons.summary: Turn a batch of comments and DMs into on-brand, individually appropriate reply drafts you can review and send quickly, without a generic copy-paste response.
lessons.goal: Draft individually appropriate, on-brand replies for a batch of real comments and DMs in one pass, ready for a final human read before sending.
lessons.whyItMatters: Engagement is often the most time-consuming, least strategic part of the job — dozens of comments a day, each needing a reply that sounds like the brand and actually responds to what was said, not a copy-pasted 'thanks for your comment!' A prompt that processes a batch of real comments at once, in brand voice, with escalation flags for anything sensitive, turns an hour of manual replying into a few minutes of review and send.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a batch of real comments or DMs ready to paste, plus a short brand voice guide (tone words, anything the brand never says, how it typically signs off).
steps: Collect a batch of comments/DMs you need to respond to (5-15 at a time works well).
Note your brand voice guide — tone, what to avoid, sign-off style.
Use the reply-drafting prompt below with the batch pasted in.
Read every drafted reply against its original comment before sending — do not bulk-approve without reading.
Flag anything the prompt marks as needing escalation (complaints, legal/safety concerns, sensitive topics) and route it to a human decision-maker instead of auto-replying.
Send approved replies, editing lightly for anything that still reads slightly generic.
Note any comment type that came up repeatedly, since a recurring question may be worth a pinned post or FAQ instead of individual replies.
lessons.prompt:
Draft replies to this batch of comments/DMs in our brand voice.

Brand voice guide: [e.g., "warm, direct, a little playful, never use corporate phrases like 'we appreciate your feedback,' sign off with our first names when it fits"]

Comments/DMs (numbered):
[PASTE EACH COMMENT/DM, ONE PER LINE, NUMBERED]

For each one, write a specific reply that responds to what that person actually said — do not write a generic reply that could apply to any comment. Keep replies short and conversational, matching the platform's typical reply length.

Separately, flag any comment that should NOT get an auto-drafted reply and instead be escalated to a human for individual judgment — this includes complaints, safety or legal concerns, sensitive personal situations, or anything angry or ambiguous enough that a wrong-toned reply could make it worse. For flagged items, write "ESCALATE" instead of a draft reply, and briefly say why.
lessons.explanation: Requiring every reply to respond to what that specific person said — not a generic acknowledgment — is what keeps a batch of replies from reading like an obvious form response, which erodes trust faster than replying slowly would. The escalation flag is the essential guardrail: complaints, safety concerns, and emotionally charged comments are exactly where a wrong-toned automated-sounding reply does real brand damage, so those get routed to a human instead of an AI draft going out unreviewed. Numbering the batch keeps the input/output mapping clean so nothing gets missed or answered out of order.
lessons.example:
Comment 3: "Ordered this two weeks ago and it still hasn't shipped, really disappointed." Comment 7: "Obsessed with this color, when's it restocking?"

Expected output: comment 7 gets a specific, on-voice drafted reply about restock timing (or a note to check, if unknown); comment 3 is flagged "ESCALATE — shipping complaint, needs order-specific info and a human tone check before replying," not a generic apology reply auto-generated without knowing the actual order status.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, take a real batch of 5-10 recent comments or DMs and run this prompt, then read every draft before sending anything.
lessons.expectedResult: A batch of individually specific, on-brand reply drafts ready for a final human read, with genuinely sensitive items clearly flagged for escalation instead of auto-drafted.
commonMistakes: Bulk-sending drafted replies without reading each one against its actual comment first.
Letting a complaint or sensitive comment get an auto-drafted reply instead of being escalated.
Using replies so generic they could apply to any comment, which reads as obviously automated.
Ignoring repeated question patterns that would be better solved with a pinned post or FAQ than individual replies every time.
lessons.proTip: When the same question shows up three or more times in one batch, that's a signal to create a saved reply or FAQ post — don't keep re-drafting the same answer individually every day.

lessons.title: Turn analytics numbers into a narrative report with ChatGPT
lessons.summary: Turn raw platform analytics into a clear report that explains what happened and why, grounded strictly in the numbers you provide instead of confident-sounding guesses.
lessons.goal: Turn a set of raw analytics numbers into a client- or team-ready report that explains what happened and offers a grounded, clearly-labeled hypothesis for why — without inventing causes the data doesn't support.
lessons.whyItMatters: Clients and internal stakeholders don't just want a table of numbers — they want to know what happened and why, in plain language. But 'why' is exactly where AI tools tend to confidently invent causal explanations the data doesn't actually support ('engagement dropped because of algorithm changes'). A report that clearly separates observed facts from labeled hypotheses keeps you credible and keeps the client's trust when a stakeholder asks a follow-up question you can't fully answer from the numbers alone.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have your raw analytics numbers ready — reach, engagement, follower growth, top and bottom performing posts — for the reporting period, plus any context you know about (campaigns run, posting changes, external events).
steps: Export or gather the raw numbers for the period (reach, engagement rate, follower change, top/bottom posts).
Note any context you actually know about — a campaign that ran, a posting frequency change, a platform outage, a relevant news event.
Use the reporting prompt below, feeding in the numbers and known context separately.
Review the 'possible explanations' section and remove any that feel like a stretch beyond what the data or context supports.
Add your own professional judgment to any hypothesis before it goes to a client — the AI's guess needs your read on whether it's actually plausible.
Send the report with the facts and hypotheses clearly still separated, not blended into one confident narrative.
Save the report format so each period's report is easy to compare against the last.
lessons.prompt:
Turn these analytics numbers into a report explaining what happened this period.

Period: [DATE RANGE]
Numbers: [PASTE: reach, impressions, engagement rate, follower change, top 3 posts by performance, bottom 3 posts by performance, any other metrics tracked]
Known context (things that actually happened this period): [PASTE: campaigns run, posting frequency or format changes, external events, platform changes you're aware of — or write "none known"]

Write the report in two clearly separated sections:
1. "What happened" — a factual summary of the numbers only, comparing to the prior period if I've given you that data. No interpretation here, just what the numbers show.
2. "Possible explanations" — grounded hypotheses for the changes, but ONLY connecting to context I actually gave you or patterns visible in the numbers themselves (e.g., "the top post was a carousel, and carousels also outperformed last period" is fine; "this is likely due to an algorithm change" is not, unless I told you one happened). Label anything speculative clearly as a hypothesis, not a fact. If you don't have enough context to explain a change, say so directly instead of guessing.

Keep the tone clear and professional, suitable to send to a client or team lead.
lessons.explanation: Splitting the report into a purely factual section and a clearly-labeled hypothesis section is the core guardrail — it stops the natural drift where an AI-written report states a guessed cause with the same confidence as an observed number, which is exactly what erodes trust when a client later asks a probing follow-up. Restricting hypotheses to context you actually supplied, or patterns visible in the numbers themselves, keeps explanations honest rather than reaching for the generic 'algorithm change' excuse that isn't verifiable. Explicitly permitting 'I don't have enough context to explain this' as a valid answer is what keeps the report credible instead of always sounding certain.
lessons.example:
Numbers: reach down 18% this period, engagement rate up slightly, follower growth flat, top post was a founder-story video, bottom posts were three product-announcement carousels. Context: posting frequency was reduced from 5x/week to 3x/week this period due to a team member being out.

Expected output: "What happened" states the 18% reach drop, flat engagement rate note, and top/bottom post pattern as plain facts. "Possible explanations" connects the reach drop to the known reduced posting frequency (explicit context given), and notes the founder-story format outperforming product carousels as a visible pattern worth testing further — without inventing an unrelated algorithm-change explanation that wasn't part of the given context.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT account, pull real analytics numbers from a recent reporting period and run this prompt, then edit the 'possible explanations' section down to only what you'd actually stand behind if a client pushed back.
lessons.expectedResult: A two-part report with facts and hypotheses clearly separated, where every explanation is traceable to context you actually provided or a pattern visible in the numbers, and any unexplained change is honestly flagged rather than guessed at.
commonMistakes: Letting a hypothesis get stated with the same confidence as a factual number in the final report.
Accepting a generic 'algorithm change' explanation with no supporting context.
Skipping your own professional review of the hypotheses before sending the report to a client.
Not comparing to the prior period's numbers, which makes 'what happened' hard to interpret as better or worse.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running context log of everything that happens each period — campaigns, format changes, team changes, platform outages — even a one-line note per event. Feeding real context in is what makes the 'possible explanations' section genuinely useful instead of empty.

lessons.title: Generate campaign visuals with ChatGPT and Gemini
lessons.summary: Produce a consistent set of on-brand campaign visuals across formats using ChatGPT's GPT Image 2 (or Gemini's native image generation as an alternative), with a brief that locks style and composition so the whole set looks like one campaign.
lessons.goal: Generate a coherent set of campaign visuals across multiple formats (square, story, banner) using ChatGPT's GPT Image 2 or Gemini's native image generation, styled consistently enough to read as one campaign rather than unrelated images.
lessons.whyItMatters: Campaign visuals need to work across a square feed post, a vertical story, and sometimes a wide banner — and they need to look like they belong to the same campaign at a glance. Both GPT Image 2 (in ChatGPT) and Gemini's native image generation produce inconsistent results between separate prompts unless the brief locks down a specific, repeatable style description; without that, a manager ends up with visuals that all look like they came from different projects. GPT Image 2 is the stronger all-round pick for prompt adherence across a full set; Gemini's native image generation is a solid alternative, especially for infographic-style visuals or when you want to keep editing the same image conversationally instead of regenerating from scratch each time.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a ChatGPT or Gemini account and your campaign brief — the campaign name/theme, brand colors, and which formats you need (square, story/vertical, banner). This lesson uses ChatGPT's GPT Image 2 as the primary path, with Gemini's native image generation as an alternative.
steps: Write down the campaign's core visual theme in one sentence, plus your exact brand colors.
Decide which formats you need (square feed post, vertical story, wide banner, etc.) and their dimensions.
Use the campaign-visual prompt below in ChatGPT (or Gemini), defining one locked style description you'll reuse across every format.
Generate the first format and treat it as your style anchor — check it against your brand guide before generating the rest.

Regenerate the remaining formats using the identical style description, changing only composition/dimension — in Gemini you can also do this conversationally by asking it to re-edit the same generated image into a new aspect ratio, which can hold consistency even tighter than a fresh prompt.
Lay out all generated visuals side by side to check for consistency in color, mood, and style before finalizing.
Add any required text overlay in a separate design tool for legibility rather than relying on in-image text.
lessons.prompt:
Generate a set of campaign visuals that need to look like one consistent campaign across formats.

Campaign theme: [ONE SENTENCE, e.g. "summer product launch, bright and energetic"]
Brand colors: [YOUR EXACT COLORS/HEX CODES]
Style description (I will reuse this exact wording for every format): [e.g., "flat vector illustration style, bold color blocking, one clear subject, minimal detail, no gradients"]
Subject/concept for this visual: [WHAT SHOULD BE SHOWN]

Generate this as: [FORMAT, e.g. "a square 1:1 feed image" / "a vertical 9:16 story image" / "a wide banner"], with a clear focal point and negative space suitable for a text overlay I'll add separately.

Avoid: in-image text (I'll add real text separately), any color outside my stated palette, extra decorative elements not tied to the subject, a different rendering style than what I specified.

After this one, I'll ask for the same style description in a different format/dimension — keep the style description identical each time so the set matches. (If you're doing this in Gemini, you can instead say "now regenerate the same image as a vertical story crop, keeping everything else identical" to edit the same visual conversationally rather than starting over.)
lessons.explanation: Writing one fixed style description and reusing its exact wording across every format generation is the core technique for visual consistency — small variations in phrasing between separate prompts are what cause a set of 'campaign visuals' to look like they came from three different campaigns. This works in ChatGPT thanks to GPT Image 2's strong instruction-following, and in Gemini you get a second lever: since its native image generation supports conversational editing, you can ask it to reformat the exact same generated image rather than generating a fresh one from a text description each time, which can hold consistency even tighter. Naming exact brand colors rather than a vague mood word keeps every generated image inside the actual brand palette instead of the tool's default color choices. Planning for text overlay in a separate design tool sidesteps inconsistent text rendering between formats, keeping the campaign's actual message legible.
lessons.example:
Campaign theme: summer product launch, bright and energetic. Colors: coral #FF6B4A and cream #FFF6E9. Style: flat vector illustration, bold color blocking, one subject, no gradients. First format: square feed image, subject a single stylized sun icon with the product silhouette.

Expected output: three visuals (square, vertical story, wide banner) all rendered in the same flat vector style with coral and cream color blocking, the same subject treatment scaled to each format's composition, each with genuine negative space left for the campaign's real headline text to be added afterward — reading clearly as one connected campaign rather than three unrelated images, whether generated fresh each time in ChatGPT or edited conversationally from one source image in Gemini.
lessons.exercise: In ChatGPT or Gemini, generate a square, a vertical story, and a banner visual for one real or practice campaign using the identical style description across all three, then lay them side by side to check consistency.
lessons.expectedResult: A set of campaign visuals across your required formats that visibly share the same style, color palette, and subject treatment, ready for text overlay in a separate design tool.
commonMistakes: Slightly rewording the style description between formats, causing visible drift in the final set.
Letting the AI render campaign headline text directly instead of adding legible text separately.
Approving formats individually without laying the full set side by side to check for consistency.

Switching between ChatGPT and Gemini mid-campaign without re-anchoring the style description first — the two models interpret the same wording slightly differently, so pick one tool for a given campaign's set rather than mixing outputs.
lessons.proTip: Save your locked style description as a standing template for the whole campaign duration — reusing the identical wording for every asset request, including later mid-campaign additions, is what keeps a campaign visually consistent for its full run. If you're on Gemini, keep the original generated image in the same chat thread so you can keep editing it into new formats conversationally instead of restarting from the text prompt each time.

lessons.title: Manage multi-client workflows: templates, voices, and approval flows with Claude
lessons.summary: Build a repeatable system for running multiple client accounts — separate voice profiles, reusable prompt templates, and a clear approval flow — so switching between clients doesn't mean starting from scratch or mixing up brand voices.
lessons.goal: Set up a documented multi-client system — a voice profile per client, a shared set of reusable prompt templates, and an approval checklist — that prevents brand-voice mix-ups and speeds up switching between accounts.
lessons.whyItMatters: Managing several client accounts at once creates a specific, high-stakes failure mode that solo-brand work doesn't: sending a comment reply, caption, or report in the wrong client's voice, or missing a client's approval step because the workflow wasn't documented. A structured system — a distinct voice profile per client, prompt templates that force the client name and voice to be specified every time, and a written approval flow — turns multi-client management from a constant risk of mix-ups into a repeatable, auditable process.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Have a list of your current clients, a short voice/style note for each (even rough), and your current approval process for each one (who signs off, on what, before what goes live).
steps: List every active client and, for each, write a short voice profile: 3-5 tone words, phrases they never use, and their typical CTA style.
Note the current approval requirement for each client (e.g., "captions need sign-off, replies don't" or "everything needs client approval before posting").
Use the system-design prompt below to turn this into a standing reference document per client.

Build your working prompt templates (captions, replies, reports) to always require you to name the client explicitly before generating anything — never run a prompt for 'the client' without specifying which one.
Ask Claude to generate a pre-send checklist that includes a client-name confirmation step, to catch mix-ups before anything goes out.
Test the system for one week across at least two clients and note any point where you almost sent the wrong voice or skipped an approval step.
Refine the weakest point in the checklist based on that real test, not hypothetically.
lessons.prompt:
Help me build a multi-client content system that prevents brand-voice mix-ups and missed approvals.

My clients and their voice profiles:
[PASTE FOR EACH CLIENT: name, 3-5 tone words, phrases/words they never use, typical CTA style, any hard rules (e.g., "never mentions competitors by name")]

Approval requirements per client:
[PASTE FOR EACH CLIENT: what needs sign-off before posting, who approves it, typical turnaround]

Build:
1. A one-page voice-profile reference card per client, formatted identically across all clients so I can quickly compare and switch between them.
2. A standing rule I should put at the top of every future prompt: always name the exact client before asking for any content, and never let a draft go out without matching it against that client's voice card.
3. A pre-send checklist that includes, as its very first item, confirming which client this content is for and pulling up their specific voice card — before checking tone, facts, or anything else.
4. A simple approval-tracking format (a table or log) I can reuse to note what's pending, approved, or posted per client.

Keep all four things simple enough that I'll actually use them daily, not an elaborate system I'll abandon after a week.
lessons.explanation: Putting the client-name confirmation as literally the first checklist item — before tone, before facts, before anything else — targets the actual highest-risk failure in multi-client work: producing correct, well-written content for the wrong client. Formatting every voice card identically makes fast client-switching possible without re-reading a differently structured document each time, which matters when you're moving between five accounts in one sitting. Explicitly asking for something simple enough to use daily is a deliberate guardrail against over-engineering a system that looks impressive but gets abandoned within a week, which is the realistic risk with any new process.
lessons.example:
Clients: 'Client A — playful, short sentences, never says "utilize," CTA is usually a question' and 'Client B — formal, industry-expert tone, never uses emoji, CTA is always a link to book a call.' Approval: Client A needs sign-off only on captions; Client B needs sign-off on everything before it's scheduled.

Expected output: two identically formatted one-page voice cards, a standing prompt-prefix rule requiring the client name every time, a checklist starting with "1. Confirm client name and pull their voice card" before any tone or fact check, and a simple pending/approved/posted tracking table with a column for which client each row belongs to.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude account, build voice profiles and an approval checklist for at least two of your real current clients using this prompt, then use the checklist for every piece of content you send for those clients over the next week.
lessons.expectedResult: A standing reference document per client and a working pre-send checklist that starts with a client-confirmation step, tested across at least two clients for one full week with any near-miss noted and fixed.
commonMistakes: Skipping the client-confirmation-first step and checking tone or facts before confirming which client the content is even for.
Building an elaborate system with too many steps to realistically follow every day.
Letting voice cards go stale after a client's brand guidelines change without updating the reference document.
Not testing the system on a real week of work before assuming it's solved the mix-up risk.
lessons.proTip: The moment you catch a near-miss — a draft almost sent in the wrong client's voice — write down exactly what step would have caught it, and add that specific step to your checklist. A checklist built from real near-misses is far more effective than one designed hypothetically.
